title: Preferences for and attitudes towards street flowers and trees in Sapporo, Japan
research_questions: Which of three factors (tree presence, plot type, and flower bed elements) is most influential on deciding preferences for different street-planting models?
Which flower bed elements and type of flowers are most preferred?
What are the attitudes of residents towards street flowers?

methodology.participants: 81 residents of Sapporo (25 students, 56 others; 52% men, 48% women; majority in their 20s, followed by self-owned detached housing residents, students as largest occupational group).
methodology.design: Mixed-methods, combining evaluation of photomontage simulations with a questionnaire survey.
methodology.stimuli: 59 photomontage simulations of street-planting models, based on photographs taken in Sapporo residential areas (1999-2000). All photos had the same background, only planting models differed. Three experiments (A, B, C) varied tree presence, plot type (long/short), and flower bed elements/characteristics (soil, grass, hedge, flowers; color, height, arrangement, composition).
measures: Preference ratings: 5-step rating scale ('strongly like' (5) to 'strongly dislike' (1)) for each photomontage.
Attitude ratings: 14 structured items related to perceptions of and attitudes to street flowers, rated on a 5-step rating scale ('strongly agree' (5) to 'strongly disagree' (1)).
analysis: General Linear Model (ANOVA) for preferences, investigating influence of plot, trees, and their interactions.
Scheffe's multiple comparison procedure (P < 0.05) for mean score comparisons.
t-test for differences in preferences based on personal characteristics (occupation, gender, age).
Factor analysis (Varimax rotation, principal components, eigen values > 1) for attitude variables.

findings.antecedent: Presence of trees in street-planting models
findings.mechanism: Trees contribute significantly to the aesthetic quality of streetscapes.
findings.quote: Trees: Not present (2.39 a), Present (3.45 b). F-value Exp. A: 274.75***
effect_size_assumptions: Direction is unknown from p-value alone; returned d is magnitude only.

findings.antecedent: Long plot type for street-planting models
findings.mechanism: Longer plots may offer a more continuous and visually appealing planting area.
findings.quote: Plot: Not present (1.51 a), Short (2.87 b), Long (3.07 c). F-value Exp. A: 83.44***

findings.antecedent: Flowers as a flower bed element (compared to soil, grass, hedge)
findings.mechanism: Flowers are perceived as more aesthetically pleasing and contribute to visual appeal.
findings.quote: Flower bed (exp. A): Not present (1.51 a), Soil (1.97 b), Grass (2.64 c), Hedge (3.32 d), Flowers (3.97 e). F-value: 226.17***

findings.antecedent: Low and ordered compositions of brightly coloured flowers (e.g., purple Petunia sp.)
findings.mechanism: Ordered arrangements suggest compactness and tidiness, which are preferred, while bright colors are visually appealing in urban streetscapes.
findings.quote: Purple (Single, Low, Ordered) mean 3.61 c. F-value Exp. B: 48.98***

findings.mechanism: Tall flowers were found neither attractive nor appropriate for streetscapes, potentially due to concerns about reducing drivers' visibility and appearing unordered.
findings.quote: Height: Low (3.14 b), Tall (2.68 a). F-value: 35.00***

findings.mechanism: Bright colors are preferred over delicate ones, possibly due to the predominance of grey in streetscapes, making bright colors stand out.
findings.quote: Colour: Delicate (2.79 a), Bright (3.03 b). F-value: 9.10**

findings.mechanism: Ordered arrangements are preferred over chaotic ones, suggesting a preference for tidy and compact compositions.
findings.quote: Arrangement: Chaotic (2.58 a), Ordered (3.24 b). F-value: 70.97***

findings.mechanism: Flowers are seen as directly contributing to the aesthetic quality of a street.
Viewing flowers provides psychological benefits, leading to a more relaxed state.
Flowers provide visual cues that mark the progression of seasons, connecting people to natural cycles.
findings.quote: Help to make us aware of seasonal changes (mean 4.43)

findings.consequent: Provision of pleasant scents and colours
findings.mechanism: Multi-sensory input from flowers (visual and olfactory) contributes to a positive environmental experience.

findings.consequent: Feeling of safety for pedestrians (by separating from traffic)
findings.mechanism: Vegetation acts as a physical and psychological barrier, enhancing perceived safety.
findings.quote: Separate pedestrians from traffic, giving a feeling of safety (mean 4.11)

findings.consequent: Preference for photomontages (Exp. A, B, C)
findings.mechanism: Students tended to give higher ratings than other respondents, possibly due to their background in landscape architecture and horticultural science.
Men tended to rate photomontages depicting neither trees nor flowers (soil/grass, chaotic appearance) higher than women, though overall these images were rated low.

findings.consequent: Agreement with 'street flowers make the street look beautiful'
findings.mechanism: Women tended to agree more than men with statements related to aesthetic and psychological benefits of street flowers.

findings.consequent: Agreement with 'street flowers give each street individuality, and could act as a symbol for the street'
findings.mechanism: Women tended to agree more than men with statements related to aesthetic and psychological benefits of street flowers.

findings.consequent: Agreement with 'street flowers separate pedestrians from traffic, giving a feeling of safety'
findings.mechanism: Women tended to agree more than men with statements related to aesthetic and psychological benefits of street flowers.

findings.consequent: Agreement with 'street flowers help prevent bicycles being left'
findings.mechanism: Different age groups may have varying practical concerns or perceptions of street flower utility.

limitations: The study used photomontage simulations, which may not fully capture real-world perceptions.
The sample size for some demographic analyses was small.
The study was conducted in Sapporo, Japan, and cultural/geographical differences may limit generalizability to other regions or cultures.
The low ratings for tall flowers might be influenced by specific species used (Althea rosea) and concerns about driver visibility, requiring further inquiry.
The study did not fully consider drivers' preferences regarding street flower height.
